Impact of contextual factors on deviations between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements - Statistical model

Author

Sietse de Vries

Summary

This file describes statistical models to investigate whether contextual factors significantly affect the differences between light measurements at eye-level and on the body (chest and wrist).

Personal light exposure measurements were collected at multiple sites as part of the MeLiDos project, following the protocol described by Guidolin et al. (Guidolin et al. 2024). The dataset of each site is available on GitHub:

  • BAUA, Dortmund, Germany (Broszio, Zauner, and Spitschan 2025)

  • FUSPCEU, Madrid, Spain (Baeza Moyano et al. 2025)

  • IZTECH, Izmir, Turkey (Didikoglu et al. 2025)

  • KNUST, Kumasi, Ghana (Akuffo et al. 2025)

  • RISE, Borås, Sweden (Nilsson Tengelin et al. 2026)

  • THUAS, the Hague, the Netherlands (Aerts et al. 2025)

  • TUM, Munich, Germany (Hilden et al. 2025)

  • UCR, San Pedro, San José, Costa Rica (Sancho-Salas et al. 2026)

The datasets were previously imported, filtered, and combined (see SWV_data_import.qmd and SWV_data_preparation.qmd). The resulting dataset consists of hourly log‑transformed differences between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements (logdif_x = log10(MEDI_x + 0.1) − log10(MEDI_h + 0.1), where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter), and various categories describing contextual factors: activity context (act_context), light context (lightsource_primary and lightsource_secondary), photoperiod (photoperiod.state), and environment (environment).

Research questions

Main research question: Are mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn (chest or wrist) dosimeter measurements systematically dependent on the measurement context?

Subquestion 1 (comparative): Do mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ across contexts?

  • Null hypothesis: For each pairwise comparison of context-specific mean log‑transformed differences between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements, the two means are equal.

  • Rationale: If the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements do not differ across contexts, the mean deviations can be considered context-invariant, and contextual information does not need to be considered when interpreting body-worn measurements.

Subquestion 2 (absolute): Under which contexts do the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ significantly from zero?

  • Null hypothesis: For each context, the mean log‑transformed difference between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements is zero.

  • Rationale: If the results from subquestion 1 indicate that the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements depend on context, it becomes relevant to characterize the mean deviation under each context. Testing context-specific means against zero, i.e. the value corresponding to identical measurements at both dosimeter positions, allows identifying under which contexts body-worn dosimeters exhibit systematic deviations and assessing the direction and size of those deviations.

Model development

The following modeling decisions were made.

  • The dataset has a nested structure: hourly measurements were collected over multiple days for each participant, and each participant participated at only one site. Consequently, observations are not independent, and measurements taken on the same day, by the same participant, or at the same site are expected to be correlated. To account for these correlations, a hierarchical mixed-effects modeling framework with random effects was specified. Random intercepts were included for site, participant within site, and day within participant. Hour of day was considered as an additional grouping factor, but was not included because observations at the same clock hour across different participants and days are not expected to share correlated variability beyond what is captured by the day-level random effect. Moreover, residual diagnostics indicated only weak short‑range temporal autocorrelation, providing no strong justification for including an hour‑level random effect or temporal correlation structure. Random slopes were not included, as the primary aim was to estimate population‑level context effects rather than individual‑specific differences in context responses.

  • The log‑transformed differences between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements were defined as the outcome variables. The distributions of these differences show a sharp central peak and long tails, indicating leptokurtosis (kurtosis test: 9.65 for logdif_c and 14.38 for logdif_w). Initial tests using a standard linear mixed-effects model (LMM), which assumes Gaussian residuals, revealed violations of the model assumptions, as evidenced by a clear S-shaped pattern in QQ plots and heteroscedasticity in residual diagnostics. Therefore, it was decided to adopt a Student-t residual distribution, as it better accommodates heavy-tailed residuals and hence is expected to be more consistent with the observed data characteristics.

    As the measurements were recorded simultaneously at the eyes, chest, and wrist, the two outcome variables (logdif_c and logdif_w) share the same eye-level term by construction. Hence, the differences between chest and eye-level and between wrist and eye-level are not fully independent. Modeling both outcomes jointly was explored, but resulted in convergence errors due to the additional model complexity. Moreover, as the dependence between the two differences is considered to have minimal impact and is deemed largely outside the current scope, a separate model was fitted for each outcome variable.

  • The dataset includes information on the context under which the measurements were conducted, organized into four categories: activity context (act_context), light context (lightsource_primary and lightsource_secondary), photoperiod (photoperiod.state), and environment (environment). As measurement deviations between dosimeter positions are primarily driven by the lighting conditions and participant posture (De Vries, Mardaljevic, and Duijnhoven In press, In press) under which the measurements were performed, considerable overlap exists between these categories. For example, being outdoors typically makes daylight the most prevalent light source. Whether a participant was outdoors can be inferred from activity context, light context, and environment. Hence, to avoid multicollinearity, not all contextual categories should be implemented in a single model. To this end, three models were developed with different contextual factors. In these models, these factors were defined as fixed effects, as the aim was to estimate and compare measurement deviations under these specific, predefined contexts rather than to generalize to a broader population of contexts. The models (and their rationale) are:

    1. Simple model: environment * photoperiod

      The simple model was built using only photoperiod.state (day/night) and environment (indoor/outdoor) as contextual factors. While environment also had a variable called other_env, this category consists of observations with both indoor and outdoor measurements, or with missing contextual data, and accounts for only 14.38% of the data. Thus, it was decided to exclude observations with this variable. An interaction between environment and photoperiod.state was also included, as the effect of environment on measurement deviations is not expected to be constant across photoperiods. For example, outdoor daytime conditions are primarily characterized by daylight, whereas outdoor nighttime conditions are characterized by electric lighting. Based on the discussed random effects, outcome variables, and fixed effects, the following model formula was defined:

      logdif_x ~ environment * photoperiod.state + (1 | site / Id / day)

      where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter.

    2. Detailed model: activity * photoperiod

      The detailed model extends the simple model by incorporating a more detailed description of the environmental context. Rather than only specifying whether the participants were indoors or outdoors, this model instead includes the type of activity (act_context). While the variables in this category also indicate whether the participant was indoors or outdoors, it provides more contextual information on the specific activity. Although the act_context category has 5 variables (home, working_indoor, road_vehicle, outdoor_act, and other_act), only observations with one of the first four were implemented as the other_act variable represents a combination of undefined or miscellaneous activities.

      TBD: Removal of other_act, since this variable does account for 21.4% of the data.

      The formula for the model was defined as:

      logdif_x ~ act_context * photoperiod.state + (1 | site / Id / day)

      where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter.

    3. Indoor lighting model: indoor work lighting contexts

      In my simulation studies (De Vries, Mardaljevic, and Duijnhoven In press, In press), I characterized the impact of generalized indoor (office) lighting conditions (electric ceiling-based lighting and daylighting from a vertical window or lighting from a screen) on the differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeters. Building on this, it would be relevant to investigate whether similar effects are present in the current real-world datasets. This was done by filtering for measurements recorded while participants reported to be working indoors, and subsequently comparing conditions based on the primary light source: 1) electric lighting, 2) daylighting, or 3) display lighting. The conditions were saved as variables in a column called light_context. A limitation of this filtering approach is that participants may have also worked from home (and indicated this as working indoors), and thus it does not strictly consider only office environments. A model that further subdivided categories based on the secondary light source was also considered, however, this was not continued due to the limited number of observations available.

      No interaction with photoperiod is specified, as the occurrence of “daylight” as a light source inherently explains the photoperiod. The formula for the model was defined as:

      logdif_x ~ light_context + (1 | site / Id / day)

      where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter.

  • Several modeling frameworks were considered to accommodate the nested structure of the data through random effects and the heavy‑tailed distributions of logdif_c and logdif_w through a Student-t residual distribution. Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were considered; however, the implementation of a Student‑t residual distribution is not straightforward, as this distribution does not belong to the exponential family typically underlying GLMMs. Bayesian hierarchical models were also considered, as they naturally allow the specification of heavy-tailed distributions. However, a frequentist framework was preferred to retain direct test statistics and p-values for reporting, and because more resources were available to support model development. Therefore, a generalized additive model (GAM) framework (with random effects) was adopted. Although all fixed effects in the proposed models are categorical, implying a linear mean structure, the GAM framework supports Student‑t residual distributions while retaining a mixed‑effects formulation. Hence, the GAM was not used to model nonlinear predictor effects, but rather as a general framework for mixed-effects modeling with heavy-tailed residuals.

library(here)       # used to import the formatted data
library(mgcv)       # used for GAM fitting
library(emmeans)    # used to calculate marginal means and for testing
library(gt)         # used to make tables
library(ggplot2)    # used for plotting
library(tidyverse)
load(here("processed_data", "ALL_hcw_proc.RData"))

# Drop other_env category (for simple model)
ALL_hcw_hourly <- ALL_hcw_hourly |>
  filter(environment != "other_env")

# Drop other_act category (for activity model)
ALL_hcw_hourly <- ALL_hcw_hourly |>
  filter(act_context != "other_act")

# Filter for indoor measurements and create light_context variable (for indoor lighting model)
ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work <- ALL_hcw_hourly |>
  filter(act_context == "working_indoor")

ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work <- ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work |>
  mutate(
    light_context = case_when(
      lightsource_primary == "Electric light source indoors" ~ "electric",
      lightsource_primary == "Daylight indoors" ~ "daylight",
      lightsource_primary == "Emissive display light" ~ "display"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(light_context)) |>
  mutate(
    light_context = factor(
      light_context,
      levels = c("electric", "daylight", "display")
    )
  )

ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work |>
  ungroup() |>
  count(light_context, name = "n_observations") |>
  mutate(perc_observations = paste0(round(n_observations / sum(n_observations) * 100, 2), "%")) |>
  left_join(
    ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work |>
      ungroup() |>
      distinct(light_context, Id) |>
      count(light_context, name = "n_participants"),
    by = "light_context"
  ) |>
  gt()
light_context n_observations perc_observations n_participants
electric 1713 52.82% 82
daylight 1293 39.87% 71
display 237 7.31% 28

Fit and evaluate models

Models were fitted in R (version 4.5.2) using the mgcv package (1.9-4). Random effects were implemented using random‑effect smooths (bs = “re”). Because mgcv does not use the lme4-style formula syntax (i.e. site / Id / day), the structure was specified using grouping factors rather than nesting operators. Each participant was observed at only one site, having a unique ID, so the participant’s random effect was implicitly nested within site by study design. Measurement day was not unique across participants, and therefore day‑within‑participant was represented by a constructed grouping factor that explicitly nested days within participants.

# Create a nested category for Id/day
ALL_hcw_hourly$Id_day<- interaction(ALL_hcw_hourly$Id, ALL_hcw_hourly$day, drop = TRUE)

ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work$Id_day<- interaction(ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work$Id, ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work$day, drop = TRUE)

# Convert Id to factor
ALL_hcw_hourly$Id <- factor(ALL_hcw_hourly$Id)

ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work$Id <- factor(ALL_hcw_hourly_indoor_work$Id)

# Create a fodel to save the fitted models
dir.create(here("models"), showWarnings = FALSE)

Models were fitted using the bam() function with the fast restricted maximum likelihood (fREML) method, as using gam() with the standard restricted maximum likelihood (REML) method resulted in substantially longer computation times given the dataset size (approximately 10,000 observations). A comparison between the two approaches showed that fixed-effect estimates agreed to three decimal places (maximum absolute difference < 0.001 log₁₀ units).

Both models converged successfully with a Student-t residual distribution (chest: ν = 3, σ = 0.23; wrist: ν = 3, σ = 0.325). The estimated degrees of freedom reached the lower bound of the scat() family (ν = 3), indicating residuals at least as heavy-tailed as a t₃ (3 degrees of freedom student-t) distribution.

The estimated random-effect structures differed between the two models. For the chest model, site-level variance was estimated at approximately zero, indicating no differences between sites after accounting for participant-level variation. For the wrist model, site-level variance was non-zero, suggesting some site-specific variation, though this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the limited number of sites. Participant-level and day-level random effects were substantial in both models, indicating considerable between-participant and within-participant day-to-day variability.

The models explained 12.8% of deviance (or “the generalization of variance that works for non-Gaussian models”) for the chest model and 15.6% for the wrist model, indicating that most of the variability is not captured by the contextual factors or the nested structure. However, considering the inherent fluctuations in (real-world) personal light exposure measurements, this level of deviance is in line with expectations. The present analysis focuses on characterizing mean deviations between dosimeter positions across contexts, rather than predicting individual measurements. Accordingly, though individual measurements remain highly variable, the models provide relevant estimates of changes in the mean differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements.

The residual diagnostics for both models are shown in Figures Figure 1 and Figure 2. The following observations can be made regarding the plots in these figures:

  • The QQ plots for both models look similar, though the chest appears less well matched. The center of the residual distribution fairly closely follows the reference line, indicating that the model’s mean structure is adequate. In the tails, the residuals deviate from the reference line (though with a somewhat limited magnitude and symmetrically), indicating that the observed residuals are somewhat heavier-tailed than the fitted scat(ν = 3) distribution. This could be a consequence of ν = 3 being the lower bound of the scat() family, meaning the model cannot represent heavier tails, even when the data may require them.

  • In the residuals vs. linear predictions plot, the spread of residuals is fairly uniform across the range of fitted values. However, a slight funnel shape is visible, which could indicate mild heteroscedasticity.

  • Both histograms of residuals confirm the model family choice, as the residuals appear to approximate a Student-t distribution.

  • In the response vs. fitted values plots, there appears to be some structure, as the variability in responses increases for higher fitted values.

TBD: So the model fit clearly has some limitations. The question is whether the current fit is still valid to do an analysis of population-level means for each context. I’ve discussed this with a colleague who has more experience with statistics and looked for GAM diagnostics interpretation in literature. The bottom line is that my experience with GAM models is limited, so while I can find arguments for why these models can still be adequate for generating such mean estimates, I cannot fully judge whether these arguments are strong/well reasoned. So I think it is important to discuss this during our meeting, and I’m very curious about your thoughts!

Both models converged successfully with a Student-t residual distribution (chest: ν = 3, σ = 0.226; wrist: ν = 3, σ = 0.316). As with the simple model, the estimated degrees of freedom reached the lower bound of the scat() family (ν = 3), indicating residuals at least as heavy-tailed as a t₃ distribution.

As in the simple model, the estimated random-effects structures differed between the two models. Site-level variance was estimated to be approximately zero in the chest model, whereas the wrist model indicated some site-specific variation. Participant-level and day-level random effects were substantial in both models, indicating considerable between-participant and within-participant day-to-day variability.

Deviance for the chest model was 14.2% and for the wrist model 18%, both slightly higher than for the simple models.

Differences in eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements between contexts (comparative)

Subqestion 1 was formulated as: “Do mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ across contexts?”

Using the fitted models and the emmeans package (2.0.1), estimated marginal means of the log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements were computed for each combination of the fixed effects (contextual predictors). To identify if there are significant differences between the marginal means under each context, all combinations were compared using model-based t-tests (targeted contrasts). Confidence intervals and p-values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction (Jafari and Ansari-Pour 2018) to account for repeated testing.

Simple model: environment * photoperiod

In the simple model there are only environment (indoor or outdoor) and photoperiod.state (day or night) as contextual factors. This results in four contrasts:

  1. day * (indoor vs outdoor)

  2. night * (indoor vs outdoor)

  3. outdoor * (day vs night)

  4. indoor * (day vs night)

# Computing the estimated marginal means for each combination
emm_logdif_c <- emmeans(m1_logdif_c, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w <- emmeans(m1_logdif_w, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)

# Specifying the Bonferroni correction
k <- 4  # number of contrasts per outcome
ci_level <- 1 - 0.05 / k  # = 0.9875

# Extract contrasts with manual Bonferroni adjustment
get_contrast_df <- function(emm_obj, by_var) {
  ct <- contrast(emm_obj, method = "pairwise", by = by_var)
  
  # Raw (unadjusted) summary
  ct_summary <- as.data.frame(summary(ct))
  
  # Bonferroni-adjusted CIs (widened to 98.75%)
  ct_ci <- as.data.frame(confint(ct, level = ci_level))
  
  ct_summary |>
    left_join(
      ct_ci |> select(all_of(c(by_var, "contrast", "lower.CL", "upper.CL"))),
      by = c(by_var, "contrast")
    ) |>
    # Manual Bonferroni adjustment of p-values
    mutate(p.value = pmin(p.value * k, 1))
}

# logdif_c results
env_photo_c_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_c, "photoperiod.state") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_c", context = as.character(photoperiod.state))

photo_env_c_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_c, "environment") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_c", context = as.character(environment))

# logdif_w results
env_photo_w_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_w, "photoperiod.state") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_w", context = as.character(photoperiod.state))

photo_env_w_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_w, "environment") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_w", context = as.character(environment))

# Combined table of results
contrast_table <- bind_rows(
  env_photo_c_df,
  photo_env_c_df,
  env_photo_w_df,
  photo_env_w_df
) |>
  mutate(
    estimate = round(estimate, 3),
    ci_low_95 = round(lower.CL, 3),
    ci_high_95 = round(upper.CL, 3),
    p.value = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))
  ) |>
  select(
    outcome,
    context,
    contrast,
    estimate,
    ci_low_95,
    ci_high_95,
    p.value
  )

contrast_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    outcome = "Outcome",
    context = "Context",
    contrast = "Contrast",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    ci_low_95 = "CI low",
    ci_high_95 = "CI high",
    p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "95% CI", columns = c(ci_low_95, ci_high_95)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, ci_low_95, ci_high_95), decimals = 3)

Because the mean log difference represents the magnitude of the systematic deviations between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements, differences in the mean log difference across contexts indicate context dependence of these deviations. The differences are shown in Table 1. For chest-worn dosimeters, only one contrast was significant: the mean log difference differed between measurements in outdoor and indoor environments during daytime (0.058 log₁₀ m-EDI, p < 0.001). The other three contrasts were non-significant and small in absolute magnitude (difference estimate ≤ 0.036 log₁₀ m-EDI), indicating that the mean deviation between eye-level and chest-worn measurements is largely invariant across contexts. This does not imply the absence of deviations between both measurement positions, but rather that for chest‑worn dosimeters, the mean deviation shows little contextual dependence. In contrast, for wrist‑worn dosimeters, all tested contrasts were statistically significant, demonstrating that deviations from eye‑level measurements differ across contexts. Consequently, this indicates that contextual factors may be relevant when interpreting data from wrist‑worn dosimeters.

Detailed model: activity* photoperiod

In the detailed model, the contextual factors are act_context (home, working_indoor, road_vehicle, or outdoor_act) and photoperiod.state (day or night). This results in the following combinations:

  1. day * (home vs working_indoor)

  2. day * (home vs road_vehicle)

  3. day * (home vs outdoor_act)

  4. day * (working_indoor vs road_vehicle)

  5. day * (working_indoor vs outdoor_act)

  6. day * (road_vehicle vs outdoor_act)

  7. night * (home vs working_indoor)

  8. night * (home vs road_vehicle)

  9. night * (home vs outdoor_act)

  10. night * (working_indoor vs road_vehicle)

  11. night * (working_indoor vs outdoor_act)

  12. night * (road_vehicle vs outdoor_act)

  13. home * (day vs night)

  14. working_indoor * (day vs night)

  15. road_vehicle * (day vs night)

  16. outdoor_act * (day vs night)

TBD: With 16 contrasts, the Bonferroni correction is very conservative. In my lecture notes, I found that generally for more than 5 comparisons a Tukeys range test is most appropriate. I also did the analysis below using a Tukeys range test, but that resulted in the same number of significant contrasts.

# Computing the estimated marginal means for each combination
emm_logdif_c <- emmeans(m2_logdif_c, ~ act_context * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w <- emmeans(m2_logdif_w, ~ act_context * photoperiod.state)

# Specifying the Bonferroni correction
# 6 act_context pairwise within each photoperiod (×2) + 
# 4 photoperiod within each act_context = 16
k <- 16
ci_level <- 1 - 0.05 / k  # = 0.996875

# Extract contrasts with manual Bonferroni adjustment
get_contrast_df <- function(emm_obj, by_var) {
  ct <- contrast(emm_obj, method = "pairwise", by = by_var)
  
  # Raw (unadjusted) summary
  ct_summary <- as.data.frame(summary(ct))
  
  # Bonferroni-adjusted CIs
  ct_ci <- as.data.frame(confint(ct, level = ci_level))
  
  ct_summary |>
    left_join(
      ct_ci |> select(all_of(c(by_var, "contrast", "lower.CL", "upper.CL"))),
      by = c(by_var, "contrast")
    ) |>
    # Manual Bonferroni adjustment of p-values
    mutate(p.value = pmin(p.value * k, 1))
}

# logdif_c results
act_photo_c_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_c, "photoperiod.state") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_c", context = as.character(photoperiod.state))

photo_act_c_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_c, "act_context") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_c", context = as.character(act_context))

# logdif_w results
act_photo_w_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_w, "photoperiod.state") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_w", context = as.character(photoperiod.state))

photo_act_w_df <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_w, "act_context") |>
  mutate(outcome = "logdif_w", context = as.character(act_context))

# Combined table of results
contrast_table <- bind_rows(
  act_photo_c_df,
  photo_act_c_df,
  act_photo_w_df,
  photo_act_w_df
) |>
  mutate(
    estimate   = round(estimate, 3),
    ci_low_95  = round(lower.CL, 3),
    ci_high_95 = round(upper.CL, 3),
    p.value    = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))
  ) |>
  select(
    outcome,
    context,
    contrast,
    estimate,
    ci_low_95,
    ci_high_95,
    p.value
  )

contrast_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    outcome = "Outcome",
    context = "Context",
    contrast = "Contrast",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    ci_low_95 = "CI low",
    ci_high_95 = "CI high",
    p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "95% CI", columns = c(ci_low_95, ci_high_95)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, ci_low_95, ci_high_95), decimals = 3)

For the chest, 3 out of 16 contrasts are significant (home - road_vehicle, working_indoor - road_vehicle, and road_vehicle - outdoor_act, all during the day) for the wrist 2 out of 16 (home - road vehicle during the day and day - night while doing an outdoor_act). Hence, the results from the detailed model indicate that there generally is no strong impact of contextual factors on the mean log-transformed differences between body-worn and eye-level dosimeter measurements.

TBD: If no p-value correction is applied, then still only 6/16 of the chest and 8/16 of the wrist contrasts would have been significant. In the simple model, all wrist contrasts were significant. In the detailed model, it may be the case that categories are not different enough, e.g. home and working_indoor both describe indoor environments with (possibly) similar lighting. Moreover, in the detailed model, there are fewer observations available per category, resulting in larger confidence intervals. So, based on this, I think that with the available data resolution, only the simple model is appropriate.

Indoor lighting model: indoor work lighting contexts

In the indoor lighting model, the contextual factors are only light_context (electric, daylight, or display). This results in three combinations:

  1. electric vs daylight

  2. electric vs display

  3. daylight vs display

# Computing the estimated marginal means for each combination
emm_logdif_c <- emmeans(m3_logdif_c, ~ light_context)
emm_logdif_w <- emmeans(m3_logdif_w, ~ light_context)

# Specifying the Bonferroni correction
k <- 3  # C(3,2) pairwise contrasts
ci_level <- 1 - 0.05 / k  # 0.98333

# Extract contrasts with manual Bonferroni adjustment
get_contrast_df <- function(emm_obj) {
  ct <- contrast(emm_obj, method = "pairwise")
  
  ct_summary <- as.data.frame(summary(ct))
  ct_ci      <- as.data.frame(confint(ct, level = ci_level))
  
  ct_summary |>
    mutate(
      lower.CL = ct_ci$lower.CL,
      upper.CL = ct_ci$upper.CL,
      p.value  = pmin(p.value * k, 1)
    )
}

# logdif_c and logdif_w results
ct_c <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_c) |> mutate(outcome = "logdif_c")
ct_w <- get_contrast_df(emm_logdif_w) |> mutate(outcome = "logdif_w")

# Combined table of results
contrast_table <- bind_rows(ct_c, ct_w) |>
  mutate(
    estimate   = round(estimate, 3),
    ci_low_95  = round(lower.CL, 3),
    ci_high_95 = round(upper.CL, 3),
    p.value    = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))
  ) |>
  select(
    outcome,
    contrast,
    estimate,
    ci_low_95,
    ci_high_95,
    p.value
  )

contrast_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    outcome    = "Outcome",
    contrast   = "Contrast",
    estimate   = "Estimate",
    ci_low_95  = "CI low",
    ci_high_95 = "CI high",
    p.value    = "p"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "95% CI", columns = c(ci_low_95, ci_high_95)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, ci_low_95, ci_high_95), decimals = 3)

For chest-worn dosimeters, only the contrast between electric and display lighting was significant. For wrist-worn dosimeters, both the electric-display and daylight-display contrasts were significant. Hence, these results indicate that when considering hourly mean log-transformed differences between body-worn and eye-level dosimeter measurements in indoor work environments, the prevalent light source may impact these differences.

Contextual differences in eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements (absolute)

Subqestion 2 was formulated as: “Under which contexts do the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ significantly from zero?”

Each estimated marginal mean was tested against zero using model‑based t‑tests, where a value of zero corresponds to the eye-level and body-worn dosimeters measuring the same value. A negative estimate indicates that eye-level measurements were higher than body-worn measurements. For interpretability, estimates were back-transformed to multiplicative ratios of MEDI + 0.1. Note that because of the additive offset in the log transformation, these ratios slightly underestimate raw measurement ratios at very low light levels. Confidence intervals and p-values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction (Jafari and Ansari-Pour 2018) to account for repeated testing.

Simple model: environment * photoperiod

# Computing the estimated marginal means for each combination
emm_logdif_c <- emmeans(m1_logdif_c, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w <- emmeans(m1_logdif_w, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)

# Bonferroni-adjusted test against zero + CIs
get_emm_table <- function(emm_obj) {
  # Adjusted p-values (test against zero)
  emm_test <- as.data.frame(test(emm_obj, null = 0, adjust = "bonferroni"))
  
  # Adjusted CIs
  emm_ci <- as.data.frame(confint(emm_obj, adjust = "bonferroni"))
  
  emm_test |>
    mutate(
      lower.CL = emm_ci$lower.CL,
      upper.CL = emm_ci$upper.CL
    )
}

# Get adjusted results
emm_c <- get_emm_table(emm_logdif_c) |> mutate(outcome = "logdif_c")
emm_w <- get_emm_table(emm_logdif_w) |> mutate(outcome = "logdif_w")

# Combined table of results
emm_ratio_table <- bind_rows(emm_c, emm_w) |>
  mutate(
    emmean_log = round(emmean, 3),
    
    # Back-transformed ratios using the Bonferroni-adjusted CIs
    ratio = round(10^emmean, 3),
    ratio_low_95 = round(10^lower.CL, 3),
    ratio_high_95 = round(10^upper.CL, 3),
    
    p.value = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))
  ) |>
  select(
    outcome,
    environment,
    photoperiod.state,
    emmean_log,
    ratio,
    ratio_low_95,
    ratio_high_95,
    p.value
  )

emm_ratio_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    outcome = "Outcome",
    environment = "Environment",
    photoperiod.state = "Photoperiod",
    emmean_log = "Estimate (log)",
    ratio = "Estimate (ratio)",
    ratio_low_95  = "CI low (ratio)",
    ratio_high_95 = "CI high (ratio)",
    p.value    = "p"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "95% CI", columns = c(ratio_low_95, ratio_high_95)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(ratio, ratio_low_95, ratio_high_95), decimals = 2)
# Computing the estimated marginal means for each combination
emm_logdif_c <- emmeans(m1_logdif_c, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w <- emmeans(m1_logdif_w, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)

# Prepare plot data with Bonferroni-adjusted CIs
plot_data <- bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(confint(emm_logdif_c, adjust = "bonferroni")) |>
    mutate(outcome = "Chest"),
  as.data.frame(confint(emm_logdif_w, adjust = "bonferroni")) |>
    mutate(outcome = "Wrist")
) |>
  mutate(
    ratio         = 10^emmean,
    ratio_low_95  = 10^lower.CL,
    ratio_high_95 = 10^upper.CL,
    context = paste(environment, photoperiod.state, sep = " / "),
    context = factor(
      context,
      levels = rev(c("outdoor / day",
                     "indoor / day",
                     "outdoor / night",
                     "indoor / night"))),
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("Chest", "Wrist")))

# Forest plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = ratio, y = context, colour = outcome, shape = outcome)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1,
             linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ratio_low_95,
                    xmax = ratio_high_95),
                orientation = "y",
                width = 0.2,
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_point(size = 3,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1),
    labels = c("0.4", "0.5", "0.6", "0.7", "0.8", "0.9", "1.0", "1.1")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Body-worn / eye-level exposure ratio\n(back-transformed from log10 scale)",
    y = NULL,
    colour = "Dosimeter",
    shape  = "Dosimeter",
    title  = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    legend.position    = "top",
    axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 11)
  )

The estimated marginal means are shown in Table 4 and Figure 7. For chest-worn dosimeters, only one context (outdoors during daytime) showed no significant difference from eye-level measurements (p = 0.453). In the remaining three contexts, chest-worn dosimeters recorded systematically lower measurements than eye-level dosimeters, with ratios ranging from 0.82 to 0.87 (all p ≤ 0.031). All ratios being in close range is in line with the findings in Table 1, as there was only 1 significant difference between contexts. For wrist-worn dosimeters, under all four contexts measurements were significantly lower than at eye-level (all p < 0.001). Moreover, the corresponding ratios were substantially lower than those for chest-worn dosimeters, ranging from 0.53 (outdoors during nighttime) to 0.72 (outdoors during daytime). Both indoors and outdoors the deviations were largest at night, and the effect of photoperiod was more pronounced outdoors than indoors.

Detailed model: activity* photoperiod

# Computing the estimated marginal means for each combination
emm_logdif_c <- emmeans(m2_logdif_c, ~ act_context  * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w <- emmeans(m2_logdif_w, ~ act_context  * photoperiod.state)

# Bonferroni-adjusted test against zero + CIs
# With 4 act_context levels × 2 photoperiod levels = 8 cells per outcome
# emmeans handles k = 8 correctly here since all 8 EMMs are in a single object
get_emm_table <- function(emm_obj) {
  # Adjusted p-values (test against zero)
  emm_test <- as.data.frame(test(emm_obj, null = 0, adjust = "bonferroni"))
  
  # Adjusted CIs
  emm_ci <- as.data.frame(confint(emm_obj, adjust = "bonferroni"))
  
  emm_test |>
    mutate(
      lower.CL = emm_ci$lower.CL,
      upper.CL = emm_ci$upper.CL
    )
}

# Get adjusted results
emm_c <- get_emm_table(emm_logdif_c) |> mutate(outcome = "logdif_c")
emm_w <- get_emm_table(emm_logdif_w) |> mutate(outcome = "logdif_w")

# Combined table of results
emm_ratio_table <- bind_rows(emm_c, emm_w) |>
  mutate(
    emmean_log = round(emmean, 3),
    
    # Back-transformed ratios using the Bonferroni-adjusted CIs
    ratio = round(10^emmean, 3),
    ratio_low_95 = round(10^lower.CL, 3),
    ratio_high_95 = round(10^upper.CL, 3),
    
    p.value = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))
  ) |>
  select(
    outcome,
    act_context,
    photoperiod.state,
    emmean_log,
    ratio,
    ratio_low_95,
    ratio_high_95,
    p.value
  )

emm_ratio_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    outcome = "Outcome",
    act_context = "Activity",
    photoperiod.state = "Photoperiod",
    emmean_log = "Estimate (log)",
    ratio = "Estimate (ratio)",
    ratio_low_95  = "CI low (ratio)",
    ratio_high_95 = "CI high (ratio)",
    p.value    = "p"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "95% CI", columns = c(ratio_low_95, ratio_high_95)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(ratio, ratio_low_95, ratio_high_95), decimals = 2)
# Computing the estimated marginal means for each combination
emm_logdif_c <- emmeans(m2_logdif_c, ~ act_context * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w <- emmeans(m2_logdif_w, ~ act_context * photoperiod.state)

# Prepare plot data with Bonferroni-adjusted CIs
plot_data <- bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(confint(emm_logdif_c, adjust = "bonferroni")) |>
    mutate(outcome = "Chest"),
  as.data.frame(confint(emm_logdif_w, adjust = "bonferroni")) |>
    mutate(outcome = "Wrist")
) |>
  mutate(
    ratio         = 10^emmean,
    ratio_low_95  = 10^lower.CL,
    ratio_high_95 = 10^upper.CL,
    context = paste(act_context, photoperiod.state, sep = " / "),
    context = factor(
      context,
      levels = rev(c("home / day",
                     "working_indoor / day",
                     "road_vehicle / day",
                     "outdoor_act / day",
                     "home / night",
                     "working_indoor / night",
                     "road_vehicle / night",
                     "outdoor_act / night"))),
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("Chest", "Wrist")))

# Forest plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = ratio, y = context, colour = outcome, shape = outcome)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1,
             linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ratio_low_95,
                    xmax = ratio_high_95),
                orientation = "y",
                width = 0.2,
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_point(size = 3,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2),
    labels = c("0.3", "0.4", "0.5", "0.6", "0.7", "0.8", "0.9", "1.0", "1.1", "1.2")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Body-worn / eye-level exposure ratio\n(back-transformed from log10 scale)",
    y = NULL,
    colour = "Dosimeter",
    shape  = "Dosimeter",
    title  = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    legend.position    = "top",
    axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 11)
  )

The estimated marginal means are shown in Table 5 and Figure 8. For chest-worn dosimeters, no significant differences from eye-level measurements were present when being in a road_vehicle during the day and night, and when doing an outdoor_act during the night. For wrist-worn dosimeters, differences from eye-level measurements were significant under all contexts.
